_about: How a passage is built: acrostics, refrains, inclusios, chiasms, sandwiches and outlines. 'Textual fact' means the pattern is on the face of the text; 'proposed' means a respected reading that not every scholar shares. Written for this app in its own words.

entries.title: Creation as a framework of days
entries.note: The days are often read in two triads: days 1–3 give form (light, sky and sea, land and plants) and days 4–6 fill it (lights, birds and fish, animals and humans). Day 7 stands apart. Readers differ on how literally to take the days; the pattern itself is a widely noticed feature of the text.

entries.title: The Flood as a symmetrical story
entries.note: Many scholars (for example Gordon Wenham) see the Flood story as a mirror: the waters rise for 150 days, then fall for 150 days, and the centre is 'God remembered Noah' (8:1). Exact divisions differ between readers.

entries.title: The tabernacle commanded and then built
entries.note: The instructions for the tabernacle (Exodus 25–31) are followed by a long account of its being made (35–40) in nearly the same words, and the end of the book repeats 'as the Lord commanded Moses'.

entries.title: A covenant renewal in the form of a treaty
entries.note: Many scholars compare the book with ancient suzerain treaties: introduction, history, laws, blessings and curses, and provision for succession. The comparison helps to explain the book's structure; not everyone accepts a strict parallel.

entries.title: The cycle of the judges
entries.note: The narrator describes the pattern in advance: Israel does evil, is handed over to oppressors, cries out, and a judge delivers them; then the cycle starts again. The pattern is repeated through the book with variations.

parts.label: The Lord gives them into the hands of enemies
They return to evil after the judge dies

entries.title: Job in three parts
entries.note: A prose frame (chapters 1–2 and 42:7-17) surrounds a long poem in which Job and his friends speak in three rounds, followed by Elihu and then God's speeches from the whirlwind.

parts.label: The Lord answers from the whirlwind

entries.title: The Psalter in five books
entries.note: The Hebrew Psalter is divided into five books, each ending with a doxology (41:13, 72:18-19, 89:52, 106:48; Psalm 150 closes the whole). The divisions echo the five books of Moses. Numbers here are the Hebrew/English numbering.

entries.title: A frame around a short psalm
entries.note: The psalm opens and closes with the same line: 'O Lord, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth.'

entries.title: An alphabetic acrostic
entries.note: The psalm has twenty-two stanzas of eight verses, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every verse in a stanza begins with that letter. The pattern does not show in translation.

entries.title: Acrostic psalms
entries.note: Several psalms are built so that each verse (or pair of verses) begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet: Psalms 9–10, 25, 34, 37, 111, 112, 119 and 145. Some have a letter missing or out of place.

entries.title: From lament to praise
entries.note: Psalm 22 moves from the cry of abandonment (vv. 1–21) to praise and testimony (vv. 22–31), with a turning point at the words 'you have answered me'.

entries.title: One psalm with a refrain
entries.note: Psalms 42 and 43 were originally one poem. Three times the same question comes back: 'Why are you cast down, my soul?' (42:5, 42:11, 43:5).

entries.title: A refrain for four rescues
entries.note: Four groups (wanderers, prisoners, the sick, sailors) cry to the Lord and are rescued, each marked by the same lines of refrain (vv. 6, 13, 19, 28 and 8, 15, 21, 31).

entries.title: A litany
entries.note: Every verse ends with the same line: 'for his steadfast love endures for ever.'

entries.title: The woman of worth, an acrostic
entries.note: The poem on the capable woman has twenty-two verses, each beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

parts.label: The woman of worth, an acrostic

entries.title: Five laments
entries.note: Chapters 1, 2, 3 and 4 are acrostics in the Hebrew alphabet (chapter 3 has three verses for each letter). Chapter 5 has twenty-two verses but is not acrostic.

entries.title: The Servant Songs
entries.note: Since the 1890s scholars have picked out four poems in Isaiah 40–55 about God's 'servant'. Whether they form a separate set, and who the servant is (Israel, a prophet, a future king), is debated. The New Testament applies them to Jesus.

entries.title: The fourth Servant Song in five stanzas
entries.note: The poem is often read as five stanzas of about three verses each: the Lord's announcement; the astonished onlookers; the confession of the speakers; the Servant's silent death; and the Lord's concluding word.

entries.title: Jeremiah's 'confessions'
entries.note: Five passages in which the prophet speaks to God in his own voice, in the form of laments, are often grouped as 'confessions'. The grouping is modern.

entries.title: The Aramaic chapters as a chiasm
entries.note: The section written in Aramaic is often read as a mirror: the four kingdoms in ch. 2 correspond to the four beasts in ch. 7; the fiery furnace (3) to the lions' den (6); and the two stories of a proud king (4 and 5) form the centre.

entries.title: Judgement on the nations, closing in on Israel
entries.note: Each oracle begins 'For three transgressions of ... and for four'. Eight nations are named in turn, and the circle tightens until it reaches Israel itself.

entries.title: Two halves that answer each other
entries.note: The book falls into two matching halves: a call, a response, and an encounter with foreigners (sailors in chapters 1–2, Ninevites in 3–4). The same words ('the great city', 'arise, go') recur.

entries.title: The first of five discourses
entries.note: Matthew arranges the teaching of Jesus into five long discourses, each closed with a similar formula: 'when Jesus had finished these sayings' (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). Many see a parallel to the five books of Moses.

entries.title: The Beatitudes framed by the kingdom
entries.note: The first and eighth beatitudes end with the same promise, 'for theirs is the kingdom of heaven' (5:3 and 5:10), and both are in the present tense. The others are in the future tense.

parts.label: The Beatitudes framed by the kingdom

entries.title: A story inside a story
entries.note: Mark begins the raising of Jairus's daughter, interrupts it with the healing of the woman with a haemorrhage, and then returns to Jairus. Each story illuminates the other: faith, touch and the number twelve.

entries.title: The fig tree and the Temple
entries.note: The cursing of the fig tree is split by the cleansing of the Temple. Many read the two as interpreting each other: a tree with leaves and no fruit, and a Temple with worship and no justice.

entries.title: The family and the scribes
entries.note: The story of Jesus's family coming to seize him is split by the scribes' charge that he works through Beelzebul.

entries.title: Peter in the courtyard and Jesus on trial
entries.note: Peter's denials are woven around Jesus's trial before the council. Peter denies him while Jesus confesses.

entries.title: The way section between two blind men
entries.note: This long section is framed by two healings of blind men (8:22-26 and 10:46-52). In between, Jesus three times foretells his passion and the disciples fail to understand: a journey on which they gradually learn to see.

entries.title: The journey to Jerusalem
entries.note: Luke marks the beginning with 'he set his face to go to Jerusalem' and presents a long block of teaching and parables along the way, much of it found only in Luke.

entries.title: Three parables of the lost
entries.note: The lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son share a pattern: something is lost, found, and celebrated. The third parable extends the pattern with the elder brother.

parts.label: The lost son and the elder brother

entries.title: The signs in John
entries.note: John says that he has written down signs so that readers may believe (20:30-31). The first two signs are numbered (2:11; 4:54). The usual list of seven: water to wine, the official's son, the paralytic, the five thousand, walking on water, the man born blind, Lazarus. Scholars differ on whether walking on water counts.

entries.title: The seven 'I am' sayings
entries.note: In John, Jesus says 'I am' followed by an image seven times: the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way the truth and the life, and the true vine.

parts.label: The way, the truth and the life

entries.title: The outline of Acts
entries.note: The risen Christ gives the plan of the book: witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

parts.label: To the ends of the earth

entries.title: The hymn to love
entries.note: The chapter divides naturally into three parts: love is necessary (vv. 1–3), what love is (vv. 4–7), and love endures (vv. 8–13). Some call the whole a small chiasm.

entries.title: The hymn of Christ
entries.note: Many scholars think Paul is quoting an early hymn in two stanzas: Christ's descent into humiliation, then God's exaltation of him. Whether it was an earlier hymn is debated.

parts.label: Though in the form of God he emptied himself

entries.title: The hymn to the firstborn
entries.note: This passage is often read as a hymn in two parts: Christ as firstborn of all creation, and as firstborn from the dead. The parallels between the two parts are a debated feature.

entries.title: The litany 'by faith'
entries.note: The chapter lists the heroes of Israel by repeating the words 'by faith' at the start of each example.

entries.title: Sets of seven
entries.note: Revelation is built from series of seven: seven letters, seven seals, seven trumpets and seven bowls, interleaved with visions. How the series relate (in sequence or as repeated views of the same events) is debated.

parts.label: The woman, the dragon and the beasts
The end and the new Jerusalem
